slides.title: A waggle run encodes a resource vector
body: Foragers of _Apis mellifera_ communicate a resource location through the **waggle dance**, repeated movements on the comb that contain a straight abdominal-wagging run and alternating return loops. A **vector** specifies a direction and a distance from an origin; here the origin is the hive.

Dong and colleagues filmed individually marked bees visiting a feeder 150 m away. The angle of the waggle run on a vertical comb encoded the food direction relative to the sun, while its duration encoded distance. Attending bees followed the dancer at close range.

The signal concerns a location outside the hive, rather than merely the dancer’s immediate position. Video measurements establish its spatial and temporal structure; successful communication additionally requires that followers obtain the signal and subsequently choose an appropriate flight. These are distinct experimental questions.

slides.title: Gravity supplies the reference inside the dark hive
body: A dancer on a vertical comb uses the upward direction as the reference for the sun. The waggle-run angle relative to vertical represents the resource direction relative to the sun outside. This transformation allows direction to be communicated where the sun itself is unavailable.

Dong and colleagues recorded dance angles on the crowded, uneven comb surface. They measured divergence among repeated waggle runs rather than assuming that every run conveyed an identical angle. Bees without experienced dancers produced larger directional divergence in their first dances.

Directional encoding therefore has both a reference system and a motor-precision component. A follower must translate the comb-relative angle into a flight direction using celestial information. The video experiment measures the dancer’s output; it does not identify a gravity receptor or the neurons that perform the coordinate transformation.

slides.title: A familiar compass bearing survives hive relocation
body: Von Frisch and Lindauer trained marked foragers to a feeding location and then moved the hive into an unfamiliar landscape. In their 1952 displacement experiment, the training feeder was 180 m away in a direction 30° north of west. The bees had learned this route during the afternoon.

The following morning, equally familiar scented food dishes were available in four directions in the new landscape. Arriving bees were captured immediately, preventing successful visitors from returning and recruiting nestmates. Searches favored the previously trained compass direction despite the changed terrestrial surroundings.

The result supports compensation for the sun’s movement between afternoon training and morning flight. Across related tests, cloudy conditions could prevent correct orientation when both direct sun and polarized skylight were unavailable. Landmarks and celestial cues can compete; the experiment does not imply that terrestrial information is normally ignored.

slides.title: Recruits initially fly the direction advertised in dances
body: Riley and colleagues tracked bees that had followed dances advertising an unscented feeder 200 m east of the hive. A **harmonic radar** detects a small transponder carried by the bee, allowing a trajectory to be measured outside the observation hive.

Recruits released at the hive generally flew an initially straight, eastward route. Their straight-flight sections averaged 206 m before searching began. Radar positions were acquired every 3 s, permitting a separation between directed travel and more tortuous search behavior.

The recruits had not previously visited the advertised feeder. The unscented feeding site and the experimental wind direction reduced the possibility of direct odor guidance from the destination. The trajectory supports acquisition of a flight vector from the dance, although radar cannot reveal which sensory components a follower used while attending the dancer.

slides.title: Displaced recruits retain a hive-centered flight vector
body: Riley and colleagues captured dance followers at the hive and released them 200–250 m southwest of it. This manipulation preserved the communicated instruction but changed the point from which the recruit began its flight. The real feeder was no longer 200 m east of the release point.

Displaced bees nevertheless began with an eastward straight flight, averaging 188 m before search. They did not immediately choose the new bearing from the release point toward the actual feeder. The flight instruction therefore retained its direction and approximate distance after displacement.

An **origin-dependent vector** is useful from its specified origin but leads to a different endpoint when executed elsewhere. This result separates a decoded movement instruction from immediate correction to a world location. It does not exclude later use of familiar landscape information, particularly in environments richer in recognizable landmarks.

slides.title: The dance narrows search without pinpointing the feeder
body: The straight flights of hive-released recruits ended near the advertised feeder on average, but individual endpoints differed by tens of meters. Riley and colleagues then tracked looping searches, some lasting up to 20 min and extending as far as 200 m from the feeding site.

Only two tracked recruits found the unscented feeder. A mean endpoint close to the food location therefore did not imply reliable arrival by every bee. Directional variation increased near the end of the vector flight as directed travel gave way to search.

Dance information supplies an approximate search area. Local visual or odor cues can be needed to resolve the final destination, but the unscented-feeder experiment did not manipulate every possible terminal cue. Spatial scatter and terminal failure distinguish successful long-range information transfer from precise source recognition.

slides.title: Recruits compensate for drift during crosswind flight
body: Riley and colleagues measured flight tracks together with wind velocity to distinguish movement over the ground from movement through the air. A bee exposed to a crosswind must direct its body partly into the wind if it is to maintain the advertised ground track.

In one recorded flight, ground speed was 6.8 m/s while a 3.3 m/s wind acted from a different direction. The reconstructed air velocity was 5.2 m/s. The bee’s air heading differed from its ground-track direction by approximately 28°, counteracting wind drift.

The resulting displacement followed the eastward instruction rather than the uncorrected wind-displaced heading. This establishes active compensation during recruitment flight. The wind-and-radar measurements do not isolate the visual or other feedback signals that determine the correction, and a single trajectory is not a universal wind-response calibration.

slides.title: A narrow tunnel magnifies retinal image motion
body: **Optic flow** is the movement of environmental images across the retina during self-motion. Nearby surfaces produce more angular image displacement than distant surfaces for the same translational travel. A narrow textured tunnel therefore increases optic flow without requiring a long physical flight.

Srinivasan and colleagues trained honeybees through a tunnel 6.4 m long, 11 cm wide and 20 cm high. Random black-and-white texture covered the walls and floor; a mesh ceiling allowed a view of the sky. The feeder was positioned 6 m into the tunnel.

Returning bees produced waggle dances after this short passage even when an equally short outdoor journey normally elicited round dances. The preparation separates physical distance from visual motion experienced en route. It supports a visual odometer, a mechanism estimating distance traveled, rather than an exclusively energy-based distance measure.

slides.title: Axial stripes remove the tunnel’s distance inflation
body: Srinivasan and colleagues kept the feeder at the same physical location while replacing random tunnel texture with stripes parallel to flight. **Axial stripes** change little along the flight axis, reducing the visual motion normally generated by forward travel.

A 35 m outdoor journey followed by 6 m through random texture produced waggle dances in 90% of recorded dances. With axial stripes at the same total distance of 41 m, 86.7% of dances were round dances. Without the tunnel, a feeder at 35 m elicited predominantly round dances.

Physical journey length cannot explain the difference between the two 41 m preparations. The texture control identifies optic flow as the relevant variable under these conditions. It does not establish that all visual patterns are equally effective or that energetic state never affects other aspects of dancing.

slides.title: Outdoor dances calibrate the duration–distance relation
body: Srinivasan and colleagues moved outdoor feeders between 60 and 350 m and measured the duration of each waggle phase on return to the hive. Over this range, mean waggle duration increased approximately linearly with feeder distance.

The reported calibration increased by 1.88 ms of waggle duration per meter of outdoor travel. It provided a reference for interpreting the unusually long dances produced after textured-tunnel flights. The calibration was measured independently of the tunnel manipulation.

A **calibration** relates a measured signal to a known quantity under specified conditions. It is not necessarily a universal conversion applicable to every landscape or colony. The outdoor measurements establish the relation for the tested routes and distances; they do not identify the neurons integrating optic flow or storing the resulting distance estimate.

slides.title: Six tunnel meters can signal a much longer journey
body: Srinivasan and colleagues used the outdoor calibration to interpret dances following textured-tunnel passages. A 41 m journey containing 6 m inside the tunnel produced a mean waggle duration of 528.8 ms, corresponding to approximately 230 m in the outdoor calibration.

A second arrangement placed the tunnel nearer the hive, producing only 12 m of total travel. Its mean duration was 441.2 ms, corresponding to approximately 184 m outdoors. Both preparations generated a disproportionately large distance signal despite their different outdoor approach lengths.

The close textured surfaces amplified the visually measured journey. The comparison rejects a simple account in which waggle duration reports physical meters independently of visual surroundings. These inferred outdoor distances are values from the authors’ calibration, not direct measurements of a bee’s subjective experience.

slides.title: Followers search at the distance encoded by tunnel dances
body: Esch and colleagues trained dancers to fly 3 m outdoors and then through an 8 m textured tunnel toward the south. Although the actual feeder was only 11 m from the hive, returning bees produced waggle runs averaging 358 ms.

The local outdoor calibration associated this duration with approximately 72 m. Newly recruited bees searched predominantly at a control station 70 m south of the hive rather than at the tunnel feeder. Control stations offered neither food reward nor an added scent.

For the first 30 min, the tunnel was closed: dancers did not advertise the tunnel journey and recruits did not arrive at the stations. Opening it initiated dancing and subsequent recruitment. This links the visually inflated distance signal to followers’ search behavior, rather than merely to a change in the dancer’s movements.

slides.title: Outdoor calibration differs between flight routes
body: Esch and colleagues measured outdoor dance durations separately for southern and northwestern routes. A given waggle duration corresponded to different physical distances on the two routes, even though both involved ordinary outdoor flight.

For example, 270 ms corresponded to about 52 m using the southern relation but about 157 m using the northwestern relation. The northwestern landscape generated less distance signal per physical meter than the southern landscape. A single route-independent conversion would therefore misread the dance.

The relevant quantity is accumulated visual motion shaped by the route. Terrain and viewing geometry can change the relation between optic flow and physical distance. The calibration experiment does not identify the exact contribution of every landmark, but it establishes that the environmental dependence matters when comparing advertised and searched distances.

slides.title: Northwestern recruits use their route’s visual calibration
body: Esch and colleagues repeated the tunnel recruitment test with a northwestern approach: 3 m outdoors followed by 6 m through the tunnel. The actual feeder was 9 m away, and returning dancers produced waggle runs averaging 270 ms.

Recruit searches peaked near 140 m along the northwestern route. The northwestern outdoor calibration predicted approximately 157 m, whereas applying the southern calibration would predict only about 52 m. Recruits therefore searched where a route-appropriate visual-distance interpretation placed the destination.

Stations were unrewarded, and closing the tunnel before each experiment prevented the relevant dances and recruitment. The result connects dance decoding with followers’ own visual navigation. It does not establish a permanently fixed distance dictionary: the conversion depends on the visual conditions encountered by the navigating bees.

slides.title: Natural water crossings alter the distance signal
body: Tautz and colleagues moved feeders along two routes, each 580 m long. One route crossed land, water and then an island; the other remained over land. Marked foragers were trained to follow the moving food source, including a feeder carried by boat.

For each position, returning dances were filmed and waggle-run duration measured. The experiment tested whether the tunnel-defined visual odometer also depended on natural terrain. Both routes increased physical distance without the artificial proximity of tunnel walls.

Water-crossing bees continued to signal increasing distance, but the rate of increase differed across route segments. Recruits were scarce while the feeder was over water and reappeared on the island. Recruitment success and distance encoding are related but distinct outcomes, and the habitat change can affect both.

slides.title: Waggle duration accumulates more slowly over water
body: On the land–water–island route, Tautz and colleagues measured a waggle-duration increase of 1.970 ms/m over the first land segment, 0.546 ms/m over water and 2.243 ms/m over the island. Equal increments of physical travel therefore contributed unequally to the dance signal.

Segment-specific relations captured the change more closely than a single constant slope across the whole route. An all-land comparison route lacked a corresponding water-associated flattening. The control separated a specific terrain transition from a general dependence on increasing feeder distance.

A visual odometer need not stop working over water; it can accumulate less effective image motion there. These behavioral measurements constrain the distance signal’s input dependence. They do not directly record retinal motion neurons or prove that low contrast alone accounts for the entire water effect.

slides.title: Image contrast constrains natural visual odometry
body: **Visual contrast** measures differences in image intensity that make spatial structure detectable. Tautz and colleagues photographed land and water scenes along the experimental routes and analyzed intensity variation in defined image windows.

Mean contrast was greater over land than over water. The low-contrast water segment coincided with slower accumulation of waggle duration, whereas the terrestrial segments supported larger increases. The original scene photographs retain the investigators’ measurement windows.

Contrast provides a plausible connection between natural image structure and effective optic flow. A correlation across route segments does not isolate contrast from flight height, viewing direction or surface texture. The controlled tunnel-texture experiments supply a separate intervention on visual motion, while the field measurements establish ecological dependence under ordinary foraging conditions.

slides.title: Bees can learn the orientation of polarized light
body: **Polarized light** has a preferred orientation of its electric-field oscillation, called the **e-vector**. Sakura and colleagues tested whether restrained honeybees could discriminate two e-vector directions presented from above without having to complete a navigational journey.

One direction was paired with sucrose; the perpendicular direction was not rewarded. The **proboscis extension response**, extension of the feeding mouthparts, supplied a behavioral readout of association. During ultraviolet-light conditioning, responses increased to the rewarded direction while remaining low to the other.

Head-fixed bees could also learn, supporting detection without repeated active head scanning. It does not measure an internal compass bearing or establish how this sensory discrimination is converted into the direction advertised in a dance.

slides.title: Polarization learning depends on ultraviolet stimulation
body: Sakura and colleagues repeated polarization conditioning with ultraviolet light near 350 nm, blue light near 442 nm and green light near 546 nm. Each preparation used a rewarded e-vector and a perpendicular unrewarded e-vector.

It does not mean that blue and green receptors are unimportant in other visual behaviors. slides.title: Occluding the dorsal rim removes e-vector learning
body: The **dorsal rim area** is a specialized region near the upper edge of the compound eye associated with skylight polarization detection. Sakura and colleagues painted either this region or the rest of the eye before ultraviolet polarization conditioning.

slides.title: Polarized illumination can label a learned flight route
body: Kraft and colleagues trained bees in a four-tunnel maze with one entrance and three possible exits. Each tunnel was 125 cm long, 11 cm wide and 18 cm high. Polarizing filters above the tunnels specified illumination parallel or perpendicular to the flight axis.

The rewarded exit carried the same relative polarization orientation as the entrance. Incorrect exits offered no reward; during tests, choices were measured without reward. A diffuser prevented a direct view of the sun and obscured overhead landmarks.

The preparation asks whether a bee can associate a route with a particular relationship between body axis and e-vector. It does not require an absolute geographical compass solution. Moving the illumination pattern among exits then tests the contribution of polarization against a learned preference for turning or going straight.

slides.title: Route choices combine polarization with learned turns
body: In Kraft and colleagues’ straight-ahead training condition, bees chose the rewarded tunnel on 67% of tests with the original illumination arrangement. Moving the rewarded polarization to the left exit raised left choices from 15% to 28%, but straight-ahead choices remained at 51%.

In the right-turn training condition, bees chose the rewarded right exit on 74% of tests. When its polarization was moved to the straight-ahead exit, straight-ahead choices reached 56%. Three exits gave a random-choice level of approximately 33%.

The cue relocation changed behavior, but it did not erase the learned route preference uniformly across training conditions. Polarization and motor-route memory can both influence choice. The experiment supports learned use of relative e-vector information without claiming that this cue exclusively determines every route decision.

slides.title: Polarization orientation changes the direction danced
body: Evangelista and colleagues trained bees through a 12 m textured tunnel covered by ultraviolet-transmitting polarizers and a diffuser. The diffuser removed a direct view of the sun and overhead landmarks, leaving the artificial polarization pattern as the celestial cue.

With transverse polarization, waggle runs clustered along a vertical axis on the comb. With axial polarization, they clustered along a horizontal axis. The reported mean axes were approximately 91.7° and 1.3° relative to horizontal, respectively.

The experiment links polarized flight input to the communicated direction while distinguishing an axis of possible headings from a fully disambiguated sun-referenced bearing.

slides.title: Partial solar experience supports a coarse compass
body: **Solar azimuth** is the sun’s horizontal bearing; an **ephemeris** describes its changing position over the day. Dyer and Dickinson reared bees in an incubator and allowed them to fly outside only during the late afternoon.

On a cloudy test day, these bees flew for the first time during morning and early afternoon. Their dances indicated a morning solar estimate approximately 180° from the evening azimuth they had previously experienced. Around local noon, they switched toward the familiar evening direction.

The bees therefore supplied an approximate morning reference without having directly experienced that portion of the sun’s course. The step-like pattern supports a general expectation of daily solar movement refined by experience. It differs from exact memorization of every hourly sun position and leaves the implementing neuronal computation unresolved.

slides.title: Full-day experience refines the learned solar course
body: Dyer and Dickinson compared experience-restricted bees with bees that had previously flown throughout the day. Both groups were tested under a cloudy sky, so current direct sight of the sun could not explain the difference in their dance orientations.

Fully experienced bees’ solar estimates followed the continuously changing local sun course more closely. Bees with afternoon-only experience instead used the coarse morning–afternoon pattern. The comparison separates a broad expectation about solar movement from its more precise local calibration.

The sun’s horizontal bearing changes at a variable rate with time, latitude and season; a universal constant angular-rate correction is insufficient. Experience improves the temporal reference used for navigation. The design supports learned calibration but does not isolate whether particular visual scenes, flight directions or training times supplied each component of that learning.

slides.title: Clock disruption shifts sun-compass flight bearings
body: A **circadian clock** is an internal timing system with an approximately daily cycle. Cheeseman and colleagues used 2% isoflurane anesthesia to perturb this timing system and tested subsequent sun-compass homing.

In the Southern Hemisphere, bees trained to a feeder 100 m from the hive were transported 6 km into unfamiliar terrain. Six-hour anesthesia produced an approximately 87° anticlockwise shift in vanishing bearing relative to a 30-min anesthetic control. A vanishing bearing is the direction at which a departing bee leaves the observer’s view.

A time error predicts a directional error because solar bearing depends on time of day. The shifted orientation supports this relationship, but extended anesthesia can also affect general performance. The short-anesthetic control and independent clock measurements are needed to distinguish a timing disturbance from nonspecific drug effects.

body: Zeller and colleagues traced **transmedulla neurons**, cells whose branches cross the medulla from the dorsal-rim-associated input compartment toward more medial brain regions. Dye injections from different locations provided complementary views of their branching pattern.

body: **Pigment-dispersing factor**, or **PDF**, is a neuropeptide associated with circadian signaling in insects. Zeller and colleagues combined PDF immunostaining with tracer labeling of transmedulla neurons to ask where potential timing input could meet the honeybee sky-compass pathway.

PDF-positive fibers occupied the same medulla layer as parts of the traced neurons. At higher magnification, labeled puncta lay in close proximity along their passage through the medulla. The two labels did not colocalize, and PDF labeling was not found within the MEDRA itself.

The result identifies neighboring neuronal populations and a candidate site for modulation. Close proximity does not establish peptide release, a postsynaptic PDF receptor or a functional synapse. Circadian compass correction is therefore a proposed role of this contact region rather than a demonstrated action of PDF on these neurons.

slides.title: Serotonin and GABA lie near compass-pathway branches
body: Zeller and colleagues combined transmedulla tracer labeling with antibodies against **serotonin**, a monoamine signaling molecule, and **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid. GABA commonly contributes inhibitory signaling, but its action at a particular connection requires receptor and physiological evidence.

Serotonin-positive puncta overlapped the dorsal portion of the relevant medulla layer but not the MEDRA. GABA-positive fibers lay near transmedulla branches throughout their length, including the MEDRA. In both preparations, tracer and transmitter labels marked different populations rather than the same cells.

These spatial relationships support candidate modulatory and local processing interactions. They do not establish whether serotonin increases or decreases compass-pathway excitability or whether a particular GABA receptor or chloride conductance mediates an effect. The necessary receptor identity, synaptic direction and time-dependent physiology remain unmeasured in this anatomical study.

slides.title: Tubercle outputs reach bulbs and the central body
body: Held and colleagues traced the honeybee sky-compass network using dye injections, neuropil labeling and single-cell preparations. **TuLAL1 neurons** project from the anterior optic tubercle toward paired synaptic regions called the lateral and medial **bulbs**.

A second class, **TL neurons**, connects these bulbs with the lower division of the **central body**, part of the central complex. The labeled branches establish two parallel anatomical routes from tubercle outputs toward central-brain circuitry associated with directional processing.

The bulbs provide a defined interface rather than an undifferentiated relay. The study identifies its neurons and terminal organization, but it does not directly record a honeybee heading code or demonstrate the conversion of that code into a waggle-run angle. Functional interpretations must remain separate from the measured projection anatomy.

slides.title: Bulb microglomeruli organize convergent synaptic tissue
body: A **microglomerulus** is a compact synaptic complex in which a large presynaptic terminal contacts several smaller postsynaptic processes. Held and colleagues stained honeybee bulb tissue for **synapsin**, associated with presynaptic machinery, and filamentous actin, prominent in postsynaptic regions.

Confocal images revealed separated microglomerular complexes in the lateral and medial bulbs. Traced TuLAL1 terminals occupied the presynaptic cores, while postsynaptic processes from TL neurons contacted them. Complementary labeling linked cell projections to the local terminal organization.

The stains identify an anatomical arrangement for distributing tubercle signals among downstream neurons. Confocal proximity alone cannot resolve every membrane contact, so the authors also used electron microscopy. These structures are a measured substrate for parallel processing, without establishing what exact directional information each complex carries during flight or dancing.

slides.title: Electron microscopy resolves bulb synaptic contacts
body: Held and colleagues used transmission electron microscopy to examine honeybee bulb complexes at membrane resolution. Large TuLAL1 terminals contained vesicles and multiple presynaptic specializations facing smaller profiles. **Vesicles** are membrane-bound structures that store releasable signaling molecules.

The authors identified **dyadic** and **tetradic** contacts, where one presynaptic specialization faced two or four postsynaptic profiles. GABA immunostaining associated downstream TL neurons with an inhibitory transmitter phenotype. These observations constrain connectivity more directly than a light-microscopy overlap.

Synaptic morphology establishes physical contacts, and transmitter staining supports a candidate sign of downstream signaling. Neither observation identifies all postsynaptic receptors or the activity-dependent effect on a navigation computation. A GABA-associated projection is not sufficient evidence for a specific chloride-channel mechanism at every terminal in the network.

slides.title: Electric fields can mechanically deflect bee antennae
body: Greggers and colleagues recorded electric fields around dancing bees and measured antennal movements during controlled electrical stimulation. Charged bodies can exert forces on nearby charged structures; detecting such a force does not require a dedicated electric-field receptor.

An isolated wing oscillating at 40 Hz, 2 mm from the head, evoked larger flagellar movements when charge was preserved rather than discharged. Laser Doppler measurements quantified these movements. **Johnston’s organ**, a mechanosensory organ in the antennal pedicel, responded to field-induced movement. The flagellum is the distal antennal segment, and the pedicel is its supporting joint region.

The resulting sequence is an electric force, antennal displacement and activation of movement-sensitive sensory neurons. This supports a mechanical route for field detection. It does not establish that electric fields are necessary for natural dance decoding or identify the mechanotransduction channel converting movement into receptor current.

slides.title: Antennal interventions reduce learned field responses
body: Greggers and colleagues paired an electric-field stimulus with sucrose and tested the conditioned proboscis extension response. Uncharged material or an inactive stimulus source served as the unrewarded comparison. Bees learned both constant fields and modulated stimulation at 60 Hz.

After learning, removing antennae eliminated the learned field response. Wax treatments that restricted antennal joints strongly reduced it; coating surfaces while retaining movement produced a less marked reduction. Learned responses to electric cues were also retained after 24 h.

The intervention pattern supports a contribution from antennal mechanoreception, including receptors associated with both joints. It does not isolate Johnston’s organ as the sole sensor or exclude every contribution from antennal surface hairs. The conditioning demonstrates a usable cue under controlled conditions, rather than its exclusive or necessary role in a crowded hive.

slides.title: DL-Int-1 is GABA-positive and inhibited by pulse trains
body: Ai and colleagues recorded intracellularly from identified honeybee interneurons while a mechanical stimulator vibrated the antennal flagellum. **DL-Int-1** branches in the dorsal lobe and related mechanosensory tissue. Dye filling and anti-GABA staining associated this cell type with a GABAergic phenotype.

The stimulus carrier was 265 Hz, within the wing-vibration range relevant to waggle dancing. Pulse trains with durations up to 16 ms and intervals up to 33 ms suppressed DL-Int-1 firing below its spontaneous level. Longer 100 ms intervals allowed intermittent spikes during the train.

This response distinguishes closely spaced vibration pulses from more widely spaced events. Antibody controls supported label specificity, but GABA staining does not prove a particular inhibitory connection to another named neuron. The cellular recording establishes temporal filtering without identifying the receptor or ion channel that generates the observed inhibitory potentials.

slides.title: DL-Int-2 remains excited during dance-like vibration
body: Ai and colleagues found a different response in **DL-Int-2**, another identified interneuron in the primary mechanosensory processing region. Its soma did not coincide with the anti-GABA labeling observed for DL-Int-1; this negative label does not by itself identify its transmitter.

At a 265 Hz carrier, trains with 16 ms pulses and 33 ms intervals evoked an initial excitation followed by maintained excitation. In contrast, DL-Int-1 was suppressed during comparable short-interval stimulation. **Tonic** activity is sustained activity during a stimulus, whereas **phasic** activity is concentrated near a change such as onset.

The contrasting responses could allow pulse-train duration to influence downstream signaling. A proposed inhibitory relationship between the two cell types was supported by modeling and morphology, not by direct synaptic measurement. The recorded excitation must therefore be distinguished from a proven circuit for decoding advertised distance.

slides.title: Mechanosensory responses change as workers mature
body: Kumaraswamy and colleagues compared DL-Int-1 in newly emerged workers aged 1–3 days with foragers older than 10 days. The preparation combined intracellular recording with dye-filled morphology, allowing cell identity to be retained across the age comparison.

Gross arborization extent was similar between groups, but branch density differed in selected regions. Foragers’ responses showed a stronger contrast between spontaneous activity and vibration-evoked inhibition, giving the stimulus a more distinct temporal signature. The original reconstructions and response distributions document different levels of analysis.

Maturation can change signal processing without replacing a neuron’s overall projection pattern. Age and experience were not independently manipulated, however, so the differences cannot be assigned exclusively to dance learning. The comparison establishes developmental association rather than the cellular cause of an acquired navigational skill.

slides.title: Experienced dancers improve novices’ directional precision
body: Dong and colleagues created colonies of newly emerged workers with no experienced dancers and compared them with mixed-age colonies. Individually marked bees first danced for a feeder 150 m away; the same bees were tested again 20 days later.

Bees that could not follow experienced dancers before their first dance produced larger waggle-angle divergence and more disordered movements. Their directional precision improved by the later test. First dances in mixed-age colonies were already more precise, separating early social exposure from the act of merely performing a dance.

The result supports social contributions to dance development alongside an inherited behavioral pattern. Later improvement could reflect age, flight practice, following experience or their combination. Colony composition changes several experiences together, so the study does not isolate a single teaching interaction or a synaptic learning rule.

body: In Dong and colleagues’ 150 m feeder preparation, naive first dancers produced longer waggle runs and more waggles per run than first dancers from mixed-age colonies. The altered timing advertised a greater distance despite the common food location.

The persistence separates distance calibration from changes that become more normal with later foraging experience.

The experiment does not identify the sensory or neural mechanism storing that early calibration.

slides.title: Landscape knowledge can modify the recruit’s later search
body: Wang and colleagues tracked dance followers released either at the hive or at displaced sites within an explored landscape. The recruits had never visited the advertised food source. Harmonic radar sampled flight positions every 3 s.

Both groups first flew approximately the communicated vector. During later search, displaced recruits directed more behavior toward the real feeder location than toward the virtual endpoint obtained by executing that vector from the wrong origin. Search could therefore incorporate landscape knowledge acquired before the recruitment event.

The authors interpreted this behavior as inference of source location using map-like spatial knowledge. It does not directly record a neural map, and familiar visual guidance must be distinguished from a purely metric representation. The contrast with Riley’s sparse-terrain experiment emphasizes the separate contributions of initial vector flight and subsequent search.

items.text: Waggle-run angle specifies direction relative to the sun; duration specifies a visually calibrated distance from the hive. Vector flight and terminal source search are distinct.
Optic flow changes dance duration and recruit search distance. Tunnel texture and natural terrain prevent a universal conversion from duration to physical meters.
Bees refine the local solar course through experience. Circadian phase disruption causes sun-compass errors whose direction depends on hemisphere.
Ultraviolet-sensitive dorsal-rim input reaches the medulla, optic tubercle, bulbs and central body. Tracing establishes anatomy; candidate timing contacts require functional tests.

Antennal movement activates mechanosensory pathways. Identified interneurons filter vibration pulse trains, but their proposed inhibitory connections and distance-decoding role are not fully established.
Early social experience affects dance precision and lasting distance calibration. Familiar landscape knowledge can influence later search without replacing the initial dance vector.
